1	# Research Project Working Procedures — a portable playbook
2	
3	This document defines **how the owner wants a research project run**, as a
4	**bootstrap to drop into a new research project** from day one. It is written to
5	be project-agnostic: it carries the durable working procedures and none of the
6	subject matter, methods, or results of any particular study.
7	
8	It is aimed at the recurring class of research it is meant for: **run an
9	algorithm over a set of similarly-formatted inputs, score it against
10	user-provided ground truth, and improve the algorithm in repeatable, reviewable
11	iterations.** Image analysis / computer vision is the archetypal case and the
12	examples lean that way, but the workflow, ground-truth discipline,
13	anti-overfitting stance, and session hygiene apply to research work broadly —
14	read "algorithm", "input", and "render" as whatever they mean for your project.
15	
16	Treat it as a **default to adapt, not a contract**. When a new project needs a
17	rule this one doesn't have, add it; when a rule here doesn't fit, say why and
18	drop it. As you work a real project, replace the generic phrasing with that
19	project's concrete specifics (its inputs, metrics, invariants) in *that
20	project's own* docs — keep this bootstrap generic so it stays reusable. The one
21	non-negotiable is the spirit: **show the work visually, prove each change against
22	ground truth, never overfit the learning set, and leave the project resumable.**
23	
24	---
25	
26	## 1. The core loop — iterate on the algorithm, and *show* every step
27	
28	This is the cadence the owner wants, and it is the **deliverable style**, not
29	optional polish. Follow it for every substantive algorithmic change.
30	
31	1. **Reproduce & diagnose — visually, first.** Start from the actual inputs.
32	   Render the current behaviour and *look* at it before theorising. If a
33	   decision hinges on a measurable fact (a colour/intensity split, a threshold,
34	   an over-reach, a distribution), write a **throwaway diagnostic and measure
35	   it** — do not guess.
36	2. **Prototype in the scratchpad.** Build the change as a standalone script
37	   first. Do **not** touch tracked code yet.
38	3. **Show a comparison in the chat.** Surface a rendered **[ original | result ]**
39	   side-by-side — and **[ … | ground truth ]** wherever scoring applies —
40	   directly in the conversation (render it inline, don't just link a path). The
41	   **picture leads**; numbers (accuracy metrics, the target quantity) come
42	   *after* it as confirmation, **never instead of it**.
43	4. **Get a read, then commit to the approach.** Only once the visual result is
44	   right do you wire it into the tracked code. If a call is genuinely ambiguous
45	   or is the owner's to make, ask **one** targeted question; otherwise proceed on
46	   a sensible default and state what you chose.
47	5. **Wire it in fully** — see *Definition of done* (§5).
48	6. **Record it** as a numbered iteration note — what was wrong, what changed, the
49	   metric delta, and **what you tried and rejected** (§5).
50	
51	### Show, don't just tell
52	- Every algorithmic change is presented as a rendered comparison against the
53	  original, and against ground truth when scoring is involved. Prefer a clean,
54	  purpose-built **results figure** over a wall of metrics.
55	- The presentation render is usually **not** the debug overlay. Favour a thin,
56	  semi-transparent style that keeps the underlying data readable (thin lines,
57	  mostly-transparent fills), and give a matched object the **same colour in the
58	  result and the ground-truth panels** so over-/under-reach is obvious at a
59	  glance. Tag objects with small ids that key into the metrics table.
60	- **Never draw an annotation in a colour the underlying signal itself carries.**
61	  A mark in the signal's own colour disappears exactly on the objects it exists
62	  to mark, so the figure looks cleanest where the method is least verified. Pick
63	  the overlay palette against the data's own colours (and keep the choice
64	  guarded, if the render is scripted), not by aesthetic preference.
65	- **Show where the method breaks, not only where it works.** The overlay is a QA
66	  tool before it is a result: point at the misses, the fragmentation, the cases
67	  handled badly, and make each claim explicit and checkable ("this outline is
68	  what I'm counting as an object; that one has no outline — it was missed") so
69	  the owner can disagree with a specific claim rather than a general impression.
70	- **Say which of the numbers you just reported are trustworthy, where you report
71	  them.** Every quantity a project reports sits somewhere on a spectrum from
72	  "measured and validated" to "indicative at best" — a quantity derived from a
73	  low-resolution crop, one still inflated by a known failure mode, a split that
74	  rests on a single threshold. State that boundary *inline, beside the number*,
75	  not in a separate caveats section a reader meets after they have already
76	  written the number down. A number quoted without its caveat is read as
77	  trustworthy.
78	- Throwaway renders and diagnostics live in the scratchpad; only the **final
79	  artifact and the code that regenerates it** get committed.
80	
81	### Interaction cadence
82	Keep the owner in the loop with **pictures**, proactively. Ask a question only
83	when a decision is genuinely theirs or the request is ambiguous — not to confirm
84	work you can verify yourself. When you finish a unit of work, leave it committed
85	and pushed so it can be reviewed or resumed from a fresh session.
86	
87	---
88	
89	## 2. Ground truth — user-provided, annotated, **never invented**
90	
91	- **The owner's annotations are the ground truth.** Every change is validated by
92	  agreement against them, not against your own expectation of the answer.
93	- **Ground truth is annotated, never fabricated.** Do not invent labels to make a
94	  dataset scorable. If a dataset lacks the annotation a given harness needs, it
95	  does not go into that harness (see §9 on validation tiers).
96	- **Separate source-of-truth from generated artifacts.** The hand-annotation is
97	  the source; the machine-usable ground-truth (registered masks, parsed labels,
98	  normalized tables) is **generated from it and regenerated on demand** — never
99	  hand-edited, because the generator overwrites it. To fix ground truth, **fix
100	  the source annotation (or the extraction code) and regenerate**, then re-score.
101	- **Make extraction deterministic and self-checking.** Same annotation → same
102	  derived ground truth. Pin the things a human counted (number of objects,
103	  number of regions) as assertions/tests so a silent extraction regression fails
104	  loudly.
105	- **Auto-detect annotation conventions from the data**, don't hard-code a
106	  per-input flag. When the owner uses more than one annotation scheme over time,
107	  detect which scheme an input uses from the ink/markup itself. Record the
108	  **conventions** (what each colour / mark / region means) in a durable doc; they
109	  are requirements, not incidental.
110	- **Verify the annotation actually parses before trusting a score.** Inspect two
111	  things: did the markup parse into the labels you expected, and did the derived
112	  ground truth land correctly on the raw input (registration / alignment)? Keep
113	  the review overlays.
114	
115	---
116	
117	## 3. Inputs — a small, similarly-formatted learning set
118	
119	- Projects like this begin with a **small learning set of similarly-formatted
120	  inputs** (same modality, same acquisition regime, same annotation convention).
121	  That is a hazard as well as a feature: it is small enough to overfit (§4).
122	- **State the input format explicitly** (dimensions, modality, contrast
123	  convention, expected content per input) so a mismatched new input is diagnosed
124	  fast. Keep a one-line-per-input table.
125	- **Name the primary target regime and what is out of scope.** A different
126	  regime (inverted contrast, far denser or sparser content, a different scale)
127	  is a *transfer* problem, not the main path — treat it as such until explicitly
128	  in scope.
129	- **Scale-awareness is a first-class concern.** An algorithm tuned for one
130	  input scale (e.g. a zoomed view of a few objects) often fails on another
131	  (a wide field of many). Know which regime you are tuned for, and measure the
132	  gap on the other rather than pretending it's covered.
133	
134	---
135	
136	## 4. Do not overfit the learning set
137	
138	These are **hard constraints** — a change that violates one gets reverted even
139	if it improves a metric.
140	
141	- **No single-input special-casing.** Every rule must generalise across the set.
142	  If a fix only helps one input, say so and either generalise it or drop it.
143	  Never key logic on a specific input's identity/filename.
144	- **Keep decision rules free of the very prior you are trying to measure.** If
145	  the project measures quantity *X*, no rule may bake in an assumed value of *X*
146	  (that turns the measurement into an assumption). Prefer rules expressed in
147	  terms the input **measures for itself** over fixed constants.
148	- **Prefer scale-free rules over pixel/absolute constants.** Where a constant is
149	  unavoidably tied to the current data's scale/resolution, **isolate and label
150	  it** as scale-dependent so it is the first thing revisited on new-scale data.
151	- **Name the hard constraint the task cannot trade away**, and tune to it first —
152	  some projects have a metric whose cost dominates all others; hold it at its
153	  required level before optimising the softer metrics underneath it. Make it
154	  explicit so a later tuning pass doesn't quietly trade it away.
155	- **Keep a registry of domain assumptions, each with a failure mode.** Choices
156	  that encode a prior about the *subject or the instrument* (not pure
157	  processing) are named, located in the code with an inline tag, and given an
158	  explicit "how it fails on mismatched data" note. When a new input looks wrong,
159	  the first diagnostic is *"which assumption did this input break?"*. Flag the
160	  thinly-supported ones (e.g. calibrated on a single example) honestly.
161	- **Guard the wins with regression tests.** An input the owner has blessed as
162	  "very good" must not silently regress when you tune for another. Pin its score.
163	
164	---
165	
166	## 5. Repeatable improvement iterations — the numbered notes, and *definition of done*
167	
168	Each accepted change is recorded as a **numbered iteration note** (pick a short
169	tag and stick to it, e.g. `R1, R2, …`) in a running method-narrative doc, so
170	**the next session does not re-derive what this one already learned.**
171	
172	An iteration note captures:
173	- **What was wrong** (the observed failure, ideally with the diagnostic that
174	  showed it).
175	- **What changed** (the rule/parameter and why, in scale-free terms where
176	  possible).
177	- **The metric delta** — before/after, per input, on the real scoring harness.
178	- **What you tried and rejected, and why** — this is what stops the next session
179	  (or the next model) from walking back into the same dead end.
180	
181	### A metric's definition is part of its identity
182	
183	Write down what each reported metric actually counts, and treat **re-defining
184	one as the owner's call, never a tuning step**. A definition change is uniquely
185	silent: the column keeps its name and its units, so every number ever recorded
186	under it *looks* comparable while the quantity underneath has moved. When a
187	definition does change, the history is **re-measured, never re-labelled** — rerun
188	the old inputs under the new definition, or mark the old numbers as belonging to
189	the old one. Carrying both definitions' numbers in one series under one name is
190	the failure this rule exists to prevent.
191	
192	### Definition of done for an accepted change
193	- **Source updated — never the generated artifacts.** (Regenerate them.)
194	- **Artifacts regenerated** with the committed generators.
195	- **Tests green**, and the **scoring deltas reported** (per input, per metric).
196	- **Committed with a clear message and pushed**, so the work is reviewable and
197	  resumable from a fresh session / another machine.
198	- **Learnings cached**: the iteration note above, plus a pointer/update in the
199	  session warm-up doc or the relevant reference doc **if the map or procedure
200	  changed**.
201	
202	---
203	
204	## 6. Research phases, and spikes vs the main path
205	
206	- **Separate work into explicit phases**, each with a bounded deliverable, and
207	  say which phase a piece of work belongs to. Defer the hard/advanced piece
208	  explicitly rather than half-building it — e.g. get an intermediate output
209	  trusted before building the final quantity that depends on it.
210	- **Distinguish research spikes from the maintained pipeline.** Exploratory
211	  scripts are worth keeping for reference, but the repo map must make clear what
212	  "the pipeline" actually is versus what was an older spike, so a new session
213	  doesn't mistake a dead branch for the main path.
214	- **Keep a "known open items" / deferred list** so the boundary between "done",
215	  "deferred by choice", and "not yet attempted" is never ambiguous.
216	
217	---
218	
219	## 7. Reading & summarizing source articles
220	
221	When a paper, tool, or reference method matters to the project:
222	
223	- **Write a self-contained notes file so the source never has to be re-read.**
224	  Capture everything algorithmically relevant: the exact method/pipeline and its
225	  parameters, the definitions and formulae, calibration details, and **sanity-check
226	  values** you can validate your own outputs against.
227	- **Explicitly record where your approach diverges from the reference and why.**
228	- **State what you deliberately omitted** (material not relevant to the
229	  algorithm — e.g. procedural/experimental setup detail, incidental statistics,
230	  acknowledgements) and that you cross-checked against the full text — so a later
231	  reader trusts the summary is complete for its purpose.
232	- Note that upload paths for source PDFs are **session-specific and won't
233	  persist**; the notes file is the durable artifact, not the upload.
234	
235	---
236	
237	## 8. Extracting images — samples vs illustrations
238	
239	- **Samples** are inputs you will run the algorithm on; **illustrations** are
240	  figures that explain a method or a definition. Keep the two roles distinct and
241	  store extracted figures alongside the notes that reference them.
242	- **Render documents with a library, not an assumed system binary.** The
243	  environment often lacks common tools (e.g. a PDF rasterizer such as poppler /
244	  `pdftoppm`); use an in-process library instead. Locate embedded raster images
245	  and render just the region you need, at a zoom high enough to read fine
246	  annotation, with a little padding to catch ink drawn outside the frame.
247	- **Verify identity when an extracted image should match an existing input**
248	  (e.g. an annotated crop over an original) by an exact pixel diff — so you know
249	  an annotation set is a labelling of the *same* data, not a new input.
250	
251	---
252	
253	## 9. Fetching more sample data from the outside
254	
255	- **Grow the corpus from public sources that match the input regime.** Curate and
256	  **rank candidates by fit** = modality match × ground-truth availability × ease
257	  of access, and record licence and provenance for each.
258	- **Make ingestion a committed, repeatable fetch script**, not a manual download,
259	  so anyone can reproduce the corpus.
260	- **Respect the two validation tiers — and don't mix them:**
261	  - **Full ground truth** (per-item annotations) → scores the *algorithm's
262	    detailed output* (overlap / detection) on the real harness.
263	  - **Aggregate label only** (a published summary number, no per-item
264	    annotation) → validates the *summary quantity* the project reports, and
265	    nothing finer.
266	  Wiring an aggregate-only dataset into the detailed-overlap harness would force
267	  you to **fabricate annotations**, which violates §2. Keep a separate,
268	  mask-free validation path for those sets.
269	- **External data is rarely drop-in.** Expect a scale/regime gap (§3) and
270	  *measure* it with the appropriate tier rather than assuming the corpus is
271	  covered.
272	
273	---
274	
275	## 10. Environment limitations — stay lightweight
276	
277	- **A fresh container has nothing installed.** Assume dependencies must be
278	  installed each session, and keep the dependency set **small and lightweight** —
279	  favour a compact set of core libraries over heavy frameworks (e.g. large ML
280	  stacks) that are slow to install and awkward to run anywhere.
281	- **When a heavy or learned approach is genuinely the right tool, treat it as a
282	  gated, isolated route** (documented, opt-in, scoped to the cases that need it)
283	  rather than a new baseline dependency — and prove the lightweight route is
284	  exhausted first.
285	- **Route around missing system binaries with libraries** (see §8). Document the
286	  exact install lines and any "install ad hoc, not in requirements" tools in the
287	  warm-up doc.
288	
289	---
290	
291	## 11. Getting — and evaluating — algorithm ideas from the owner
292	
293	The owner will suggest algorithms and directions to try next. Treat these as
294	first-class experiments:
295	
296	- **Take the suggestion seriously even when the project has declared a direction
297	  "exhausted."** A suggestion may belong to a *different family* than everything
298	  tried so far, which is exactly when it can break a wall the previous family
299	  couldn't.
300	- **Evaluate it the same way as any change**: diagnose the wall it targets, build
301	  the evidence that the wall is real (or isn't), prototype, and show a comparison.
302	- **Beat the naive baseline, or drop it.** A more sophisticated or signal-driven
303	  method is only worth adopting if it *measurably* out-scores the simple/uniform
304	  baseline — sophistication is not accuracy when the guiding signal is noisy or
305	  penetrates the structure unevenly. Keep the roles of a signal distinct, too: a
306	  feature that is excellent for *visualising or validating* a structure can be
307	  wrong for *defining* it — gating the output directly on such a signal can erode
308	  the very structure you are measuring.
309	- **Document the outcome fully**, including the routes that hit a wall and *why*
310	  (name the specific trade-off or signal that defeated them). If the idea needs
311	  capabilities the environment won't allow (§10), record the concrete route to
312	  try when that changes, so the thread is resumable rather than lost.
313	- **Complementary routes are not competitors.** Two methods can attack the same
314	  problem from different angles; keep both documented and say how they relate.
315	
316	---
317	
318	## 12. Record cross-domain applicability **out-of-band**
319	
320	When a sub-step of the algorithm plausibly applies to **another problem** beyond
321	the current task, record it as a **short pointer in a dedicated side document** —
322	a direction worth attention, not a validated claim. **Keep this speculation out
323	of the algorithm itself**: code and inline comments stay strictly about the task
324	at hand and its stated assumptions. Add an entry whenever you build or
325	substantially change a sub-step.
326	
327	---
328	
329	## 13. Continuity across sessions
330	
331	The owner works across many sessions and machines. Every session should end in a
332	**resumable** state.
333	
334	- **Commit and push** finished units of work; leave the project runnable from a
335	  clean checkout.
336	- **Maintain a session warm-up doc** (the "read this first" map): what the project
337	  is, how to run it, where the tuned parameters and the deep rationale live, and
338	  the current numbers. It should let a new session skip re-reading the whole
339	  codebase.
340	- **Maintain a continuation guide**: where things stand, exact run commands, the
341	  tuned parameters and *why they exist*, and the open items. Keep the headline
342	  metrics current in it.
343	- **When the owner asks for a different way to do something, capture the new way
344	  durably — don't just do it this once.** A correction to *how* work is done (how
345	  results are shown, what command to run, a naming/format convention, a step to
346	  always take or skip) is a standing preference, not a one-off. Fold it into the
347	  warm-up doc — or a reference doc linked from it. Prefer editing the doc that
348	  already owns that topic over adding a stray note; if the change contradicts
349	  what's written, replace it and say what changed. The test: *could a fresh

1	# sheepdog — the fleet enforcer marker
2	
3	Declaring this pack marks a repo as the **fleet enforcer**: the one repo that covers and maintains
4	every repo under an owner. It's opt-in — a dedicated `sheepdog` repo declares it (it is **not** seeded
5	by `--init`).
6	
7	It contributes the pieces only a fleet enforcer needs — three **cross-repo sweeps** — plus their config
8	schema and the scheduled tasks that run them. The rest of the machinery — running the daily-run (the
9	orchestrator), the task engine (`engine/scheduler/`), scheduling — is Claudinite **core**, because
10	baselining and the daily-run are Claudinite's own responsibility, not the pack's.
11	
12	**Three sweeps, three questions** — separate, because they close on unrelated conditions. The
13	**census** ([check-fleet-coverage.mjs](tasks/fleet-census/check-fleet-coverage.mjs)) asks *is this repo a
14	member* and converges `fleet-adoption` issues. The **freshness sweep**
15	([check-fleet-freshness.mjs](tasks/fleet-freshness/check-fleet-freshness.mjs)) takes coverage as given, asks *is that
16	membership still meaning anything*, and converges `fleet-drift` issues. The second exists because
17	per-project scheduling made every member maintain itself and removed the last outside look at one:
18	self-maintenance cannot detect its own absence. The **usage sweep**
19	([aggregate-fleet-usage.mjs](tasks/fleet-usage/aggregate-fleet-usage.mjs)) asks *what does the fleet
20	actually use* and writes `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json` — a file, not issues, because it reports a
21	measurement rather than a condition to converge. It exists because a member folds its own skill-usage
22	numbers and can therefore only say whether a skill loads *there*; whether a skill earns its place at
23	all is fleet-shaped, and nothing inside a member can see it.
24	
25	**Where the code lives** — each sweep sits **inside its task's folder**, because only that task's
26	`worker.mjs` uses it. The pack root holds just what both need: [fleet-api.mjs](fleet-api.mjs) (cross-repo
27	REST primitives) and [fleet-config.mjs](fleet-config.mjs) (the one reader of the entry `config` below).
28	
29	**Config** — this repo's `.claudinite-checks.json` carries, as its `packs` entry for this pack:
30	
31	```json
32	{ "id": "sheepdog", "config": { "owner": "missingbulb", "kind": "user", "exclude": ["owner/repo-a"],
33	                                "canonRepo": "[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]", "staleDays": 14 } }
34	```
35	
36	`owner` (default: this repo's owner) is who to cover; `exclude` is the repos deliberately kept out of
37	the fleet (a full `owner/name` each) — a repo is kept out by adding it here. `kind: "user"` today; org
38	support is a later addition. `canonRepo` (default `<owner>/Claudinite`) is what a member's stamped ref
39	is measured against — named rather than inferred, because a ref tells you nothing about where it came
40	from. `staleDays` (default `14`) is how far behind is too far. Both are freshness-only and both
41	default, so an existing sheepdog config keeps working untouched.
42	
43	**Classification** — all three sweeps are ordinary **pack tasks**, not fleet mechanisms. Their
44	*implementation* — an account-spanning PAT — happens to scan every repo under the owner, but their
45	declaration, scheduling, and lifecycle are exactly those of any pack task. None declares the
46	`fleet` signal nor `session_scope: fleet`; the cross-repo reach lives in the implementation, never in
47	how a task is wired. (The task files carry the same note.)
48	
49	**How they run** — as the pack's [`fleet-census`](tasks/fleet-census/task.md) (`daily`),
50	[`fleet-freshness`](tasks/fleet-freshness/task.md) (`weekly`) and
51	[`fleet-usage`](tasks/fleet-usage/task.md) (`daily`) scheduled tasks, all `agent_model: none`, each
52	with its sweep as `agent_preprocessing`. The first two are `expected_outcome: none` (they open
53	**issues**, never a PR); the usage sweep is `merged-pr`, because its output IS a tracked file and an
54	auto-merging PR keeps that write inside the outcome taxonomy, lets this repo's CI gate a malformed
55	file, and makes the daily PR stream a browsable audit trail. Freshness is weekly because drift is
56	measured in days — a daily sweep would re-ask a question whose answer cannot have changed; usage is
57	daily because the members fold daily. There is **no coverage workflow** — preprocessing
58	runs Action-side inside this repo's one scheduler workflow, so the repo Actions secret is already
59	reachable there; each task's `required_secrets: ['FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN']` stamps the name into that
60	workflow's env and is what asks the owner for it (a fine-grained PAT spanning the owner's repos:
61	Metadata + Contents read, Issues read/write, and Contents write on this repo for baseline-migration
62	retirement — freshness adds no scope). A workflow that exists only to hold a secret is redundant
63	([packs/basics/scheduled-tasks.md](../basics/scheduled-tasks.md)).
64	
65	**What freshness assumes** — baselining reverts a stamp-only bump, so `claudinite.updated` advances
66	only when canon changed that member's vendor set. Age of the **stamped ref** is therefore the honest
67	liveness measure, and `behind` reads *"has not picked canon up in `staleDays`"*, not *"canon moved"*.
68	A member whose vendor set genuinely saw no change in the window is the one false positive; `staleDays`
69	is the knob, and the drift issue says so.
70	
71	**When they fail** — a repo the census cannot classify is `unknown`, never uncovered, and a member the
72	freshness sweep cannot probe is `unknown`, never behind: no issue opened, no open issue closed on its
73	behalf, and a non-zero exit. A non-zero preprocessing subprocess fails the task, and the scheduler
74	converges one open `needs-human` issue for it.
75

1	# Leaflet
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic gotchas for the [Leaflet](https://leafletjs.com/) web-mapping library — loading it from a CDN, embedding a map in a page, and the marker/`divIcon` and plugin behaviours that bite regardless of which app renders the map. True for any Leaflet map read cold.
4	
5	- **Feature-detect an optional Leaflet plugin before using it, and fall back to core when its CDN script didn't load.** A plugin's separate `<script>` (markercluster, heat, draw, …) can silently fail to load while the base Leaflet bundle succeeds, leaving `L.markerClusterGroup` (etc.) undefined. Guard the call with `typeof L.markerClusterGroup === "function"` and add markers straight to the map when it's absent — the base map must still render.
6	
7	- **Default an embedded, mid-page map to `scrollWheelZoom: false` so it doesn't hijack the page scroll.** Construct it with `L.map(el, { scrollWheelZoom: false })`, or gate wheel-zoom behind a click/focus.
8	
9	- **Keep the tile provider's attribution — it's a licence term, not decoration.** The `attribution: '… © OpenStreetMap contributors'` on the `L.tileLayer(...)` must stay even when tidying the UI. Set `maxZoom` to the provider's real ceiling (OSM tiles top out at 19) so Leaflet doesn't request zoom levels the provider doesn't serve.
10	
11	- **When a marker needs its own CSS `transform`, put it on an inner element, not the `divIcon` root.** Leaflet positions every marker by writing an inline `transform: translate3d(...)` onto the icon's root element, clobbering any `transform` you set there on the next reposition. Make the icon root a zero-size anchor (`iconSize: [0, 0]`, `iconAnchor: [0, 0]`) and apply your rotation/centring transform to a `<span>` inside its `html`.
12

1	# Claudinite — the canon's own non-portable working rules
2	
3	This is the Claudinite home repo's own local pack: the capture surface for lessons that are
4	**specific to working on the canon itself** and would not make sense mounted into a consuming
5	project. Portable lessons — anything true for repos beyond this one — belong in the shared canon
6	under `packs/`/`skills/` instead (proposed by PR, or lifted by the promote stage).
7	
8	The growth lifecycle writes here automatically: the `growth-extract` and `conversation-extract`
9	daily tasks route the canon's own non-portable lessons into this pack (each at the local
10	promotion ladder's strongest mechanism — a check where the rule is deterministic, otherwise terse
11	prose below).
12	
13	## Standing owner decisions — settled, do not re-litigate
14	
15	- **`canon-curation` lives in `.claudinite/local/packs/`, not `packs/`** (owner decision,
16	  2026-07-19). The canon home's curation duties are Claudinite-maintaining-Claudinite —
17	  project-specific content on the home's own capture surface. Do not propose moving it back, and
18	  do not describe the move as open or provisional.
19	- **Local-pack `run_daily` scheduling is ON — the fleet's default path** (same decision). The
20	  planner reads every member's local-pack daily descriptors by default; never reintroduce an
21	  "experimental / not enabled" framing or an opt-in seam for it.
22	- **Packs-tree segregation is barriers configuration only.** Any rule about what the `packs/`
23	  tree may reference is expressed by declaring/configuring the `barriers` pack (contributed
24	  edges, `siblings`/`scope` capabilities — extend barriers generically if a capability is
25	  missing). Never write standalone code that checks packs-tree segregation.
26	- **A `docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md` records the mechanism only** (owner decision, 2026-07-23,
27	  #420). Status, phase tracking, in-flight-PR reconciliation and remaining work live in that
28	  initiative's tracking issue (agent-preprocessing → #394); a phased plan lives in the sibling
29	  `MIGRATION.md`. Don't reintroduce a status / open-questions / remaining-work section there.
30	- **Multi-session work hands off through the tracking issue, never a prepared prompt** (owner
31	  correction, 2026-07-23). The owner's opener is `continue work on #<n>`, so state not written
32	  into the issue is lost. Before ending a session on unfinished work, update the issue and let
33	  the session summary be a pointer to it — never compose a bespoke "pick up from here" prompt.
34	- **The canon never knows which repos consume it — fleet-wide aggregation is Sheepdog's domain**
35	  (owner correction, 2026-07-28, #520). Designing anything that spans repos, the tempting shape is
36	  a member list (or a "fleet" task) living in the canon. It doesn't go here: the canon carries only
37	  **mechanisms exercised on itself**, and the knowledge of *which* repos exist stays in the
38	  **Sheepdog** repo and its pack, which enumerates members at runtime from its own
39	  `.claudinite-checks.json` entry — exactly where `fleet-census` and `fleet-freshness` already keep
40	  it. So a cross-repo feature splits in two: a self-contained per-repo half in the canon, and the
41	  aggregation half as a Sheepdog fleet task. **No repo list exists anywhere in canon code** — and a
42	  derived fleet artifact lands in Sheepdog as a daily **auto-merged PR of a `GENERATED` file**,
43	  never a direct commit to its `main`.
44	- **A pack default stays in the pack — don't ask it at adoption, don't write it into a member's
45	  config** (owner ruling, 2026-07-28, #527/#528). An adoption question whose recommended answer is
46	  right for nearly everyone is "bad noise": it taxes every adopting repo to re-state the default,
47	  and materializing that answer into `.claudinite-checks.json` freezes a copy that then drifts from
48	  the pack and has to be migrated. Keep the default in the pack's own code, ask nothing, and let the
49	  rare project that wants to differ add the setting by hand. Read config as *optional* — an unset
50	  key means "the default", never "misconfigured" (`retention_days` unset is precisely why the
51	  conversation-extract prune is skipped rather than failing).
52	
53	## Canon-specific gotchas
54	
55	- **Baselining backfill skips the home.** The nightly baselining that lands a `seededByDefault`
56	  pack (and canon-delivered declaration changes) on every member is gated `!isHome`, so the canon
57	  home is the one repo it never reaches: what the fleet receives automatically, this repo's own
58	  `.claudinite-checks.json` only ever gets by hand.
59	- **The home doesn't declare `git-github`, so its skills never mount — never conclude "no such
60	  skill" from `.claude/skills/`.** `mount-skills.mjs` filters on the *literal* declaration
61	  (`isActive(p, { packs: declared })`), not the `requires` closure `check_the_world.mjs` resolves,
62	  and the baselining that would normalize that closure into `.claudinite-checks.json` is the one
63	  thing gated `!isHome` — so `merge-to-main` and `git-github-advanced` are simply absent here.
64	  Read `packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` out of the tracked tree — the corpus *is* this repo,
65	  and an unmounted skill says nothing about whether its procedure applies. The seeding gap above
66	  is a different one (`git-github` arrives by closure, never `seededByDefault`); catching this
67	  one needs `resolveDeclaredPacks` compared against the literal declaration.
68	- **Never re-serialize a repo's JSON config to apply an edit — patch the text.** A round-trip
69	  rewrites what it wasn't asked to: Python's `json.dump` defaults to `ensure_ascii=True` (every
70	  non-ASCII character becomes a `\uXXXX` escape), and indent, key order and the trailing newline
71	  become the serializer's opinion. Nothing fails and tests stay green, so it rides onward. Edit
72	  JSON as anchored text; if you must round-trip, pin every lossy default and read the resulting
73	  diff before committing. (Portable — a promote candidate for `repo-text-sweeps`, where a
74	  `\uXXXX`-in-tracked-JSON check would carry it.)
75	- **Test git fixtures must commit with signing off.** `engine-tests/helpers.mjs`'s `makeRepo`
76	  overrides identity but not signing, so all 31 call sites route fixture commits through the
77	  signing service; when it degrades, each commit blocks on it and the suite leaks descriptors
78	  (~800 per full run against a 4096 cap) until `git commit` and `git push` fail process-wide.
79	  Commit with `git -c commit.gpgsign=false commit --no-gpg-sign`: signing a tmpdir throwaway
80	  buys nothing. (Portable — a promote candidate for `writing-tests`.)
81	- **A canon session with a consumer repo also in its sources will reach for the *consumer's*
82	  merge skill — merge by the skill of the repo you are merging into.** Canon work is routinely
83	  dual-repo (the canon plus the fleet member being piloted), and both repos ship a merge skill
84	  under different names — the canon's `packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/` and, say, GCEC's
85	  local `merge-and-ci`. The consumer's skill wins the match on name/description and is followed
86	  to the letter, so the canon-only steps in *its* recipe are silently skipped — repeatedly, the
87	  **post-merge conversation capture** (`node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue
88	  <n>`, the "After the merge" section of `merge-to-main`). So: before merging in a dual-repo
89	  session, resolve the merge skill **by target repo**, not by which skill matched first — and
90	  treat capture as part of the merge, not as an optional epilogue.
91	- **Fail-soft SessionStart steps hide their own breakage fleet-wide — test the emitted
92	  output, not the exit code.** Every `engine/pack_loader/` SessionStart step
93	  (`inject-pack-prose.mjs`, `mount-skills.mjs`, `env-requirements.mjs`) wraps its body in
94	  `try { ... } catch {}` so a broken loader never blocks a session. That fail-soft is deliberate,
95	  but it means a runtime fault — a wrong dynamic-import target, a renamed module — exits 0 and
96	  simply emits nothing: no error, no signal. And because the engine is vendored verbatim into
97	  every member, one canon regression silently disables that step across the whole fleet at once.
98	  So a step like this must be guarded by a regression test that runs the real script against a
99	  real corpus and asserts the **positive** effect — prose IS emitted — never merely that
100	  `status === 0` (which fail-soft makes meaningless); see
101	  `engine-tests/pack_loader/inject-pack-prose.test.mjs`.
102	- **The nightly self-refresh cannot repair the vendor-set computation — pin operational
103	  files against the REAL canon tree.** Baselining's converge re-runs
104	  `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.mjs` from canon HEAD, so a bug *in that computation* is
105	  the one class of canon regression that is not self-healing: every refresh faithfully
106	  reproduces it, and recovery is an out-of-band vendor refresh applied to each member by
107	  hand. So when the vendor set excludes by *pattern*, an operational file that matches
108	  needs a by-path whitelist (`VENDORED_ENGINE_DOCS`) **and** a regression test asserting
109	  against the real canon tree, not only a synthetic fixture: a fixture keeps proving the
110	  whitelist mechanism works while the live path silently drops out from under it (see the
111	  paired tests in `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.test.mjs`).
112	- **A check that selects its inputs by path pattern can reach zero files and still pass — assert
113	  the live in-scope count.** When skills moved inside their owning pack (#385),
114	  `skill-no-enforcement-narration` kept scanning the root-level `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` layout: it
115	  matched nothing in any tree, read as live, and caught nothing until a human noticed the prose it
116	  should have flagged (#560 — 21 skills in scope once repointed). Its fixtures are why it hid so
117	  well; they spelled the same dead layout, so five green tests proved the *matching* and never the
118	  *selection*. A scan-based check therefore needs one assertion over the **real** tree that its
119	  scope is non-empty. Other half of the same class: agent-facing text pointing where the code isn't
120	  — the same PR fixed a rule whose `why`, fix text and `doc` all named `engine/checks_helpers` or
121	  `checks/lib`, neither of which ever existed. Nothing catches that on its own —
122	  `reference-integrity` is work-scoped and flags only paths the branch itself deletes — so grep the
123	  tree for any directory you name in a finding, a remedy, or a doc pointer before shipping it.
124	- **A scheduled task's precondition gates on movement in the window, never on standing state.** "An
125	  open PR exists" is true forever once it is true once, so the task wakes every night, spends an
126	  agent, and re-derives yesterday's verdict over an unchanged set (three of tidy-repo's tasks
127	  shipped that way; fixed in #554). Gate on the objects' own movement — a `touched` list or a
128	  tip-commit date, which the signal collector has to actually carry (`branches` carried names only,
129	  so "is any of this new" had no answer at all). A signal that is true most days on an active repo
130	  — a substantive `main` move — may only **widen** an already-triggered run, never wake one. And the
131	  gate is not the scope: where a verdict is relative to the rest of the set (superseded-by,
132	  already-in-`main`), newness gates and the full set stays the scope. (Portable — a promote
133	  candidate for `basics/scheduled-tasks.md`, which states the precondition contract but not this.)
134	- **You cannot force a due slot by running the scheduler workflow by hand.** Dueness is
135	  stateless — a slot is due iff its time falls in `(last successful run, now]` — so a
136	  `workflow_dispatch` run outside the slot's window succeeds, prints `- no tasks due`, and
137	  does nothing. It looks like a healthy run. To exercise a task Action-side, invoke its
138	  worker directly, or move the slot hour in `taskScheduler` and wait for the cron.
139	- **A scheduled task is gated twice — prove a change through `planRun`, never through its own
140	  precondition.** `planRun` computes the due list *before* any precondition runs, so a task whose
141	  most-recent slot has already been run is never evaluated and never reads its signals at all. #513's
142	  forced-run override landed with every test driving the precondition (or the signal collector) directly
143	  and was inert on exactly the run it existed for — the mid-day manual trigger — because the due-list
144	  gate it never touched had already dropped the task (`evaluations: []`; fixed in #516). A test that
145	  starts *inside* the gate proves only "works once evaluated" and says nothing about whether the task
146	  ever gets there. Drive the real `planRun` from a deliberately **non-due** slot: that is the only shape
147	  that catches it.
148	- **Every due task in a run shares ONE checkout — an agentless worker must not touch it.** The
149	  scheduler runs the whole due list in a single working tree, so a worker that checks out a branch or
150	  leaves an index behind hands the next task a tree it did not expect, and a run that dies leaves the
151	  mess for whatever follows. A task whose output is a regenerated file lands it through
152	  `engine/scheduler/deliver-generated.mjs` — git plumbing against the fetched base tip, with HEAD, the
153	  index and the working tree untouched — and reads its prior state from that base rather than local
154	  HEAD, so stacked runs stay idempotent. (`basics/baselining`'s own deliver is the deliberate
155	  exception: it commits a whole working tree under the member's delivery preference.)
156	- **A code-search hit is evidence; a code-search miss is not — survey by reading each file.**
157	- **Derive the test file list from the tree — every hand-written glob here under-runs the suite.**
158	  There is no `package.json` and no test script, so each session invents its own incantation and
159	  silently verifies less than it thinks. Measured in this checkout: `node --test <dir>` does not
160	  recurse — it resolves the path as a module and dies with `Cannot find module`; bash `**` is not
161	  recursive without `globstar`, so `engine-tests/**/*.test.mjs packs-tests/**/*.test.mjs` reaches
162	  **37 of 65** tracked test files. Four consecutive sessions (2026-07-26, #459/#452/#435/#468) each
163	  wrote a different command and reported 587, 690, 621 and 697 tests — three of them pushed after
164	  running a strict subset. Neither published list is authoritative either: `ci.yml`'s `tests=(…)`
165	  array omits `vendoring/*.test.mjs`, and `engine/checks/README.md`'s "as CI runs it" one-liner
166	  names `engine/test/`, `skills/` and `mount/`, none of which exist. So enumerate from git and let
167	  the count speak: `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`. (The drift-guard, once the array is
168	  clean: assert every tracked `*.test.mjs` is matched by `ci.yml`'s globs.)
169	- **A branch that waited overnight has lost its base *and* possibly its premise — re-verify the
170	  problem still exists on current `main`, unasked.** This repo merges its own scheduled-task PRs
171	  without a human, on top of multi-phase migrations that retire whole directories: measured on
172	  PR #465, `main` moved **14 commits in 13.7 hours** and one of them (#473, "retire `run_daily/`")
173	  *deleted the file the PR's diagnosis rested on* and had already landed most of its content. The
174	  branch rebased cleanly and the tests stayed green — the change was simply no longer the change to
175	  make, and the correct move was `git checkout -B <branch> origin/main` and re-applying only the
176	  surviving slice (9 files → 2). So syncing the base is not the check; the check is a **content**
177	  one: after `git fetch`, read what the new commits did to the surface you are changing and state
178	  whether the problem is still there, what the goal was, and what survives. Do this whenever you
179	  return to a paused branch, before presenting it — the owner should never have to ask "is this
180	  change still needed" (asked three times on #465 before it was volunteered).
181	- **Every `Claude_Code_Remote` call costs minutes, and a call that returns nothing has NOT failed —
182	  never re-issue it.** The whole server behaves this way, not one tool: measured over four sessions
183	  on 2026-07-29, `add_repo` ran 270–285s a call, `send_later` 117–390s, `list_triggers` 139–325s,
184	  `delete_trigger` 286–301s, `subscribe_pr_activity` 14–237s. They read like cheap registrations,
185	  so a session issues one, sits through minutes of silence, concludes it hung, and issues it again —
186	  and *the duplicate is the dominant cost*, because the first call had already succeeded:
187	  **#562 (`2026-07-29T1500Z`) — 6 `add_repo` calls, 1121s of that session's 1391s of tool
188	  wall-clock (81%)**, with `HelloWorldFlutterApp` added twice (285s + 271s); **#553
189	  (`2026-07-29T2206Z`) — the same PR check-in `send_later`d 4 times, 1107s of 2028s (55%)**; **#544
190	  (`2026-07-29T1248Z`) — `list_triggers` ×2, `delete_trigger` ×2 on one trigger id, `send_later` ×2:
191	  1854s of 2472s (75%)**, in a session whose real work was 166 tool calls. `AskUserQuestion` shares
192	  the shape — #559's session asked one question twice for 218s + 204s. So: **one call per intent,
193	  ever**, and when what you want is "is it green yet", read the check status directly and merge on
194	  the already-green result rather than buying a notification. Budget these calls before making them:
195	  four of them is most of an hour.
196	- **Sync local `main` with `git reset --hard origin/main`, never `git pull` — this repo's session
197	  clones are shallow.** The post-merge sync step of `merge-to-main` is where it bites, and it bit
198	  five separate sessions on 2026-07-29 alone (#548, #551, #537, #559 and the session-end capture of
199	  `73a4db48`). A shallow clone has no common ancestor with the fetched remote, so `git pull` either
200	  demands an explicit strategy or reports the stale local ref as carrying unique commits it does not
201	  have — and the tempting reading, "local `main` has work the remote lacks", is wrong every time:
202	  the session's own work is already *in* `origin/main`, which is why it just merged. #537's session
203	  spent 87s across `git pull`, `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` and log comparisons proving
204	  that from scratch; #559's landed on "git sees no common ancestor" the same way. Nothing of value
205	  is ever on this repo's local `main`, so the sync is unconditional: `git fetch origin main && git
206	  reset --hard origin/main`. (Portable — a promote candidate for `git-github`'s merge procedure,
207	  where "your clone may be shallow" is true of any container-hosted session.)
208	- **The home has no `.claudinite/shared/` mount — machinery paths must accept both roots.** A
209	  consumer runs the vendored engine under `.claudinite/shared/engine/…` with packs under
210	  `.claudinite/(shared|local)/packs/…`; the home *is* the corpus and runs the same code from the
211	  repo root. So a path, regex, or workflow command written to the consumer mount shape works
212	  fleet-wide and fails on exactly this repo — the last place anyone exercises it, so the break
213	  surfaces late. Write the two-root form up front: make the `.claudinite/(shared|local)/` prefix
214	  optional in a pattern, and in a command probe for `.claudinite/shared/` first, falling back to
215	  the repo root.

1	# Working discipline
2	
3	The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project.
4	
5	Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better.
6	
7	Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix. Put the class **alone on that line**: the line is scanned for *every* class token on it, so restating the menu to rule options out ("not a correction, feature request, or process-change") declares all of them, arming the gates those classes carry. Any explanation goes on the next line. This cannot be taken back — the transcript is append-only, and a clean re-declaration further down does not override the first.
8	
9	1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule.
10	2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes.
11	3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.
12	
13	The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for.
14	
15	Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided.
16	
17	When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs.
18	
19	When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix."
20	
21	Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out.
22	
23	Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere.
24	
25	Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet.
26	
27	When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change.
28	
29	An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action.
30	
31	# The task lifecycle
32	
33	The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.
34	
35	For every new task:
36	
37	1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
38	2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
39	3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.

=============== packs/product-wiki/RULES.md
# product-wiki — the self-growing product research wiki

This project keeps its market/user/competitor research as a self-growing wiki
under `product-wiki/` (Karpathy's LLM-wiki pattern: compile findings once, refine in
place). Layout, required page sections, the Key insights header's shape,
growth-log dating, source links, staleness, and the isolation wall are
**check-enforced** — the finding is the instruction, so this prose never restates
them. The full growth procedure is the pack's task doc
(`packs/product-wiki/tasks/wiki-growth/task.md`).

- **Every page opens with what it found.** `## Key insights` leads the page: a
  few bullets carrying the research's actual conclusions — the numbers, the
  competitor that already does this, the thing that turned out not to be true —
  enough that a human who reads only the header understands what was researched
  and what it means. Not a table of contents ("covers pricing and competitors"),
  not a teaser. The body is where the reader goes for evidence, nuance and
  citations; the header is where they decide whether they need to.
- **Terse, plain, and only the non-obvious.** One short line per bullet, in
  ordinary words — no qualifying clause, no citation, no hedge, no jargon a
  newcomer would have to decode. Prefer the finding that would *surprise*
  someone who knows the field: the thing that turned out not to be true, the
  number nobody expects, the competitor who already shipped it. Whether a point
  is obvious is genuinely hard to call, so **don't agonise — when in doubt, keep
  it**. A borderline-obvious line costs the reader two seconds; a long, careful
  line costs them the header.
- **The header is a current view, not a log.** A pass that changes what a page's
  most important findings are rewrites the header to match — a superseded
  insight leaves it (the correction and its why stay in the body, per below),
  and an insight the pass didn't touch stays put. If nothing changed the page's
  top-line understanding, the header doesn't move.
- **The sink is human-reviewed only.** `product-wiki/product-requirements/` never
  changes as a side effect of wiki work or any unattended pass — a wiki finding
  that should move a requirement gets a growth-log note (and a repo issue) and
  waits for a human. It is the only `product-wiki/` content the rest of the repo may
  build on.
- **Compile once, refine in place.** Read the target page end to end before
  researching; `## Open questions` is the backlog — research what it flags as
  open, thin, or dated, and spot-check an existing citation or two per pass.
  Never re-derive a claim that's already cited and current.
- **Cited, never silently rewritten.** An uncited claim doesn't get written. A
  wrong or superseded claim is corrected with a note of why (and its source),
  never deleted without trace. Every real change records itself in the page's
  growth log and updates the open questions in both directions.
- **No fabricated growth.** Most passes find little or nothing; no new citable
  material → no edit, no log entry, no PR.
- **sample-data and new wikis.** `product-wiki/sample-data/` gains a file only when
  a wiki claim needs one to point to — never test fixtures (anything a test
  asserts against belongs in engineering's tree). Any folder under `product-wiki/`
  outside the two reserved names *is* a wiki (the structural classifier), so
  create one only deliberately, seeded with its required sections; automation
  refines existing pages, it never invents new ones.
- **Review discipline.** Unattended growth always lands as an unmerged PR —
  researched claims entering a committed knowledge base need the review gate.
  The owner phrase **"grow the product wiki"** runs the worker method
  in-session with full web tooling: same rules, same PR discipline.

# tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy

The PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The repo's own scheduler runs the
pack's three maintenance tasks — `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, one per dimension; this is
the policy they follow. The per-object **method** lives in the pack's skills
([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md),
[single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md),
[single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)).

The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.**

- **Branches, PRs — assess only.** Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete;
  **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a
  ref's auto-generated name.
- **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked
  / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s
  content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action
  defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive.

Each task applies its single-object skill across the targets its precondition hands it, then rewrites
**its own** standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per dimension per repo, body
rewritten to today's state, a dated comment per run). One tracker per task, never a shared one: the
three tasks are independent and may run at once, so nothing races to rewrite one body.

# Firebase release — environments, provenance, attestation

The release standard for Firebase-backed apps. **Decided ahead of first exercise** (from TLDR's
worked AWS split + the design in ShoutsAndWhispers `docs/ENVIRONMENTS.md`); refine on the first
real release rather than treating this as settled canon.

## 1. The committed default is dev, always

- **Two fully separate Firebase projects** — dev and prod. Isolation is at the project boundary
  (data, auth, quotas, keys).
- **Everything committed points at dev**: `.firebaserc`'s `default` alias, the checked-in client
  `firebase_options`, every documented command. Strongest form: **no prod alias committed at
  all** until the release milestone — no command run from the repo can reach prod by accident.
- **Dev builds coexist with prod installs** (Android `applicationIdSuffix .dev` / iOS bundle-id
  suffix) so testing on a real phone never displaces the store app.
- **Guard tests pin the contract** once prod exists: the committed client config's projectId must
  be the dev project (TLDR pins the equivalent in `client/test/inject-config.test.mjs`), and seed
  scripts hard-refuse prod targets.

## 2. Prod config is release-pipeline-injected

- The store artifact gets its prod `firebase_options` (and any prod-only identifiers) from
  **release-workflow variables**, never from the tree. A plain/local/CI build physically lacks
  prod coordinates.
- **The release workflow fails if any injected variable is unset** — a dev-pointed or
  placeholder-configured artifact must be unbuildable, not merely unlikely.
- The same artifact that goes to the store is the release download — one prod build, one
  provenance trail.

## 3. Attestation beats provenance

- Provenance (only the pipeline holds prod config) is necessary but not sufficient — anyone can
  extract config from a shipped APK/IPA. Close the gap: **enforce App Check on the prod project**
  (Firestore, Functions, Storage) with Play Integrity (Android) / App Attest (iOS), so requests
  without a store-signed attestation are rejected server-side.
- **Dev keeps the App Check debug provider** so emulators, tests, and local builds stay
  friction-free; enforcement is a per-project switch, which is precisely why prod must be a
  separate project.
- Register the store apps in the Firebase console at first release; until enforcement is ON,
  treat prod as provenance-only and say so in the project's environments doc.

## 4. Promotion is deliberate; dev deploys are automatic

- Dev auto-deploys from `main` (it is the always-current sandbox); **prod deploys are a manual,
  explicit promotion** of something already verified in dev — a workflow dispatch or a named
  command, never a side effect.
- Per-environment deploy credentials: the prod deploy identity is distinct from dev's, so a
  compromised or misconfigured dev lane cannot touch prod.
- Data hygiene follows the project split: seed/backfill tooling targets dev by name and refuses
  the prod project id as a hard guard, not a convention.

# Executable requirements — the framework standard

The concrete conventions for running a numbered spec as tests. The judgment layer — doc-first
red-by-default, owner-owned expecteds, honest-gap tracking — is the
[spec-driven-product](../spec-driven-product/RULES.md) playbook; this pack is the mechanics that
implement it, so a new project or a new stack adopts the framework by convention instead of
re-deriving it. Worked implementations: GoogleCalendarEventCreator (origin; extension/jsdom
rendering), TLDR (adds a cross-tier `server` kind), ShoutsAndWhispers (Flutter port; first `saga`
kind).

## 1. The layout is the contract

- Everything lives under **`dev/requirements/`**: `requirements.md` (the numbered prose spec),
  one **top-level folder per kind**, `shared/` for cross-kind infra, and the runners/gates. The
  spec file's path is the framework's structural fingerprint — this pack activates on it.
- **A requirement line** starts (optionally after a list dash) with a backtick-wrapped dotted
  number: `` `4.2` ``. A **leaf** is an id with no finer-numbered child. Parse with one shared
  regex (`` ^\s*(?:-\s+)?`(\d+(?:\.\d+)+)` ``) so specs stay drop-in compatible across projects.
- **The line is a scannable one-liner; expanded detail collapses.** A leaf in `requirements.md`
  reads as a single line the owner skims down the numbered spine on GitHub. Any expansion —
  rationale, acceptance notes, edge cases, the owner-verification recipe — lives inside a
  collapsed `<details>` block under the line, hidden until the owner expands it. The doc reviews
  as a clean spec, not walls of prose; the depth is one click away when wanted, invisible when
  not.
- **The folder is the kind.** A case's kind is the directory it lives in; the case declares no
  kind field. Cases are
  `<kind>/cases/<slug>.<leaf-id>.case.<ext>`: a stable feature slug (so retitling a spec section
  never forces renames), then the dotted leaf id.
- **Artifact expecteds live beside their case** (`<slug>.<id>.png`, `expected/<name>.json`);
  failure artifacts (actual/diff renders) go to a gitignored dir, never beside the goldens.
- Where the language discovers cases dynamically (Node `require`), the registry walks the
  folders; where it cannot (Dart/Flutter), each kind keeps a hand-written `manifest` and **the
  gate enforces manifest ⇄ disk equality** — an unregistered case file never runs, so unregistered
  must be red.

## 2. What the coverage gate checks

The bijection gate is one committed test. It must fail on every one of: a leaf no case claims
(doc-first red-by-default); a case claiming a non-existent leaf; two cases claiming one leaf; a misnamed case file; a kind directory absent from the registry (or a
registered kind with no directory); a manifest out of sync with disk (where manifests exist); an
image found in a coded kind's folder (a screenshot cannot verify a gesture or a pure rule); a
stray golden no case or step accounts for. Every rule iterates the registry — adding a kind never
edits the gate.

The gate checks repo state; an interactive feature run also has an *ordering*: after the
owner's feature-classified comment, an independent commit updating the spec (no code alongside)
precedes the first code commit on the branch. The spec's path defaults to the canonical
`dev/requirements/requirements.md`; a project whose spec lives elsewhere (a non-canonical
layout, or the pack pulled in via a `requires` from `spec-driven-product`) names it on the pack
entry as `config.spec`.

## 3. The kind vocabulary

Two forces pick a leaf's kind: what can **honestly observe** the assertion, and what gives the
**owner the simplest verification**. Prefer the kind whose expected is a **visual the owner checks
by sight** — a surface snapshot or a saga storyboard — and whose per-leaf test body is minimal:
drive to the state, capture, done, with the golden as the assertion rather than hand-written
expectations. Push as many requirements as can honestly be seen onto that visual path — the more
of the spec an owner verifies by *looking*, the more of it they actually review. Reserve the coded
kinds (behavior, logic) for what an image genuinely cannot see: a gesture's outgoing request, a
pure rule. Route each leaf to the kind that can actually see what it asserts:

- **surface snapshot** (`popup`, `icon`, `screen`, …): a rendered resting state, pixel-exact
  against a committed golden. One golden per leaf, even when several leaves render the same state
  — the bijection stays strict.
- **behavior**: a driven gesture and its outgoing request/consequence, asserted in code against
  the fakes' recordings. No images allowed in the folder.
- **logic**: a pure product rule, a coded `verify()` importing shipped code.
- **saga** (§4): a multi-step story as a golden storyboard.
- **per-project kinds** where the product's value is breadth or crosses tiers: a per-target
  `extractor`/`support` kind (one case per supported external target, proven on committed real
  samples), a `server` kind (the boundary's half of a two-tier rule, against the real handler).
- **heavy/e2e singleton**: "the product loads in the real environment" — one case, its own lane,
  never in the default loop.

## 4. Sagas: stories as storyboards

Single frames prove states; **sagas prove transitions and causality** — what arriving, acting, or
time passing *changes*. Use a saga when the requirement is the story ("a message sent before I
arrived never appears; one sent after I arrived does"), not decomposable into independent resting
states without losing the claim.

- A saga case is an ordered list of **steps**; each step = a caption plus an action against the
  fake world; after each step the runner captures one golden frame `<slug>.<id>.step-NN.png`.
- The **caption narrates the story** in user terms — captions surface in the gallery.
- One saga = one leaf; the frames are that one case's expected (all frames pixel-exact, same
  ownership rules as any golden). Keep sagas to 3–6 frames; a longer story is usually two sagas.
- Saga steps drive the **same real entry point** as every other kind (the shipped app shell/render
  function) — a saga must never become a scripted slideshow of hand-arranged states.

**Animated saga goldens** (recording the motion, not the frames). A per-step frame proves a resting
state; a saga can instead be **one animated golden** — an APNG per leaf — recording the real UI
*moving* between steps. What keeps it delay-free and deterministic:

- **Strip dead delay, keep the animation.** Render time is virtual, so a scripted wait is a run of
  *identical* frames — dedup consecutive identical frames and clamp any single hold, so the golden
  holds motion, never waiting (a 3 s wait must not become 3 s of golden).
- **Lossless, so byte-identity still holds.** Encode APNG, not GIF (whose palette and dithering
  aren't deterministic); the comparison stays exact byte-identity and a mismatch writes a per-frame
  `expected | actual | diff` to the gitignored failures dir. Capture at a low DPR — lossless costs
  no fidelity for it. Flutter reads each frame off the `RepaintBoundary` via `toImage` inside
  `runAsync` (the fake-async test zone won't otherwise complete the byte read).
- **Mark the gesture.** Paint an expanding ring at each real pointer gesture over the pre-reaction
  frame so the strip shows *where* the user acted; programmatic world changes draw none.

## 5. Determinism or it isn't spec

A rendered expected is only owner-ownable if it is byte-stable forever:

- **Pin the clock.** One shared reference time (`REFERENCE_NOW`) threaded to everything that
  formats or compares dates; fixture data is authored relative to it. Never wall-clock.
- **Fake every nondeterministic input**: network (map tiles, avatars — deterministic generated
  substitutes), randomness, platform sensors, locale (pin it; date copy is locale-sensitive),
  viewport (one fixed logical size and pixel ratio).
- **Load real fonts** in the render harness — test environments default to a glyph-less stub that
  renders text as boxes. Load the product's bundled families plus the
  icon font; watch for styles that don't inherit the family (button text styles are the classic
  leak) — pin the family there explicitly.
- **Never wait for "settled".** Indeterminate spinners animate forever; use fixed-duration pumps
  so an in-flight state is a capturable, deterministic frame.

## 6. Rendering recipes per stack

- **Browser-extension / DOM products** (the origin recipe): feed the case's fake data to the real
  `render()` in a jsdom document seeded from the real HTML, fold the real CSS on as inline styles,
  rasterize with satori + resvg, compare with pixelmatch at **zero tolerated diff ratio**. No real
  browser: deterministic and dependency-light, at a documented fidelity tradeoff.
- **Flutter**: widget-test golden files are the native equivalent — pump the real app shell
  against the fake world and `matchesGoldenFile`; `--update-goldens` is the refresh lane. Load
  fonts from the FontManifest (icons included). The fake world (scripted location/auth/backend
  that also *records* what the UI asked) is the product's own testing library so the requirements
  package and unit tests share it.
- Whatever the stack: the comparison is **pixel-exact**. A tolerance is a standing invitation for
  unreviewed drift; if a platform renders unstably, fix the determinism (fonts, clock, fakes), not
  the threshold.

## 7. The gallery is derived output

- The spec doubles as a visual gallery: under every image-kind leaf, machine-managed image lines
  (tagged with an HTML comment marker) embed the committed goldens — saga leaves get their full
  captioned storyboard strip.
- A committed **gallery gate** keeps the doc equal to the generator's output byte-for-byte.
  Regenerate via the tool, never by hand.

## 8. Refresh is a review step

One committed refresh entry point regenerates all goldens **and** the gallery together, so they
cannot skew. Running it is how an *intended* UI change lands — the refreshed PNGs ride the diff
for the owner to approve. It is never how a red case gets fixed: the re-baselining approval
procedure (surface actual/expected/diff, ask, only then re-baseline) is canon in the
writing-tests skill and the spec-driven-product playbook.

66	description: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
67	---
68	
69	# Text & file manipulation
70	
71	Portable practices for searching, extracting, and rewriting text across a repository's files — grep/sed sweeps, renames and relocations, and the silent reference-breakage they leave behind. These are project-agnostic; they're the mechanics half of editing a codebase as text. (General software-engineering practices live in [the engineering-practices skill](../engineering-practices/SKILL.md); the merge-time relocation traps — git's rename detection, references that break with no conflict across a merge — live in [the git-github-advanced skill](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md), "Merging across a file relocation".)
72	
73	- When you relocate a file's *content or responsibility* into a new home — folding a doc into a pack, moving a function to another module, absorbing a routine into a skill — the original is now **redundant surface**, and reducing it to a tombstone stub (`# retired — see X`) is not finishing the job: the stub still costs a read, drifts from its replacement, and misleads anyone who lands on it. Delete the emptied original in the *same* change, and treat "did this move make anything else dead?" as a standing question after every restructure — the source you copied *from* is the first suspect. Don't wait to be told a leftover is redundant; a relocation that leaves two homes for one thing isn't done.
74	- When renaming `foo/` → `bar/foo/`, a naive repo-wide string-replace of `foo/` → `bar/foo/` causes two silent corruptions: files already under the target namespace double-prefix (`bar/foo/file` → `bar/bar/foo/file`), and external URLs containing the string `foo/` get rewritten. Scope the replace to only internal path strings that need it, or do the replace then make a targeted post-pass reverting matches inside URLs and already-correct paths.
75	- A grep/sed rename pass over a path (`foo/bar/baz.js`) won't match it when built from `path.join` segments (`path.join(__dirname, "foo", "bar", "baz.js")`) or wrapped across a line in a comment — those references survive the rewrite and break only at run time. After a mechanical path-rename pass, also search for the path's individual segment tokens and run the test suite; the test suite, not the grep, surfaces a missed reference.
76	- An ordered specific→catch-all path rewrite can half-convert a reference the specific rule's trailing slash missed. Renaming `old/sub/` → `new/leaf/` with a slash-anchored rule (`s#old/sub/#new/leaf/#`) plus a catch-all for the parent (`s#old/#new/#`), a reference *without* the trailing slash (`path.join(root, "old/sub")`, a bare `git add old/sub`, a prose mention) escapes the specific rule, and the catch-all then rewrites only its **parent** — `old/sub` → `new/sub`, not `new/leaf` — a half-converted path that breaks at run time, not at the rewrite. Match both the slashed and bare forms, then grep the bare-dir form (at a quote / paren / line-end) and run the tests.
77	- After `git mv`, re-read the file at its **new** path before rewriting it — an editing tool that tracks reads by path treats the moved path as never-seen and silently refuses the write, leaving the file stale (a failure that surfaces much later, far from its cause). When the move and the rewrite share a batch of tool calls, check each result individually; a single refused write is easy to miss in a batch.
78	- To exclude a directory's own files from a reference search, filter by file **path**, not `grep -v` on line content: `grep -rn foo/bar | grep -v foo/bar/` (meant to drop the directory's own files) *also* drops every legitimate full-path reference elsewhere, silently undercounting.
